source: Docs/Chapters/03_SURVEYOR_3.md: Legendas finais PT/EN (SUR-S01–S31) e Textos de UI PT/EN. Transcrição literal; chaves de UI ganham o prefixo 'sur.' para não colidir com o dossiê global.
notes: As chaves são idênticas às de surveyor.pt-BR.json (há teste). 'group': narrative, objective, dossier, hud, card (data/nome usa o carimbo). 'status': approved = transcrito do roteiro; derived = metade de uma frase aprovada, usada só para fonte ampliada.
SUR-Sxx.p1/.p2 são as duas telas de uma frase de dois períodos; juntas reconstroem o texto inteiro. Nenhum texto é narração de IA e nenhum vira frase em C#.

entries.text: Before sending people to the Moon, we needed to understand the ground they would land on.
You are Surveyor 3. Your commands come from Earth.
A radio command takes about 1.3 seconds to cross that distance.
Almost three days of travel. A small correction brings the destination closer.
Align the marker with the circle. Then hold E to send the correction.
Ocean of Storms. The next step is landing.
The radar became confused near the ground. The engines kept firing.
The team sent an engine-cutoff command. Surveyor touched the ground three times.
Now, still. The first picture is one command away.
Line by line, the Moon began to appear on screens back on Earth.
Marks in the soil tell the story of the landing.
It came to rest on a crater slope, tilted to one side.
The camera looked around using a movable mirror.
Seeing the ground was not enough. We had to touch it.
The scoop opened small trenches to reveal how the soil behaved.
Pressing showed how strongly the ground resisted.
Dropping the scoop revealed another response from the same soil.
Loose grains at the surface. Enough cohesion to hold the trench edges.
These data helped planners prepare for astronauts and their equipment.
On April 24, Earth crossed in front of the Sun, as seen from here.
A reddish rim: sunlight passing through Earth's atmosphere.
While there was daylight, it kept observing.
The long lunar night arrived. On May 4, contact ended.
It never answered again. But its images and measurements were already on Earth.
Thirty-one months passed over the same landscape.
The camera was already silent. This is the image it never got to transmit.
In November 1969, Apollo 12 landed a short walk away.
On the 20th, Pete Conrad and Alan Bean went to meet the old lander.
The camera, scoop and other parts returned to Earth for study.
The rest of Surveyor 3 remains on the Moon.
It stayed. What we learned from it came home with us.
